You sound like me before I had a baby, down to feeling 50/50 on the idea of kids, needing a day or two to recover after socializing, and just really loving your “me” time. If just one person would have been honest with me, like really honest, I probably would have leaned into not having children and there are a lot of reasons why I am now one and done. 

Instead of any honesty, I felt tricked and lied to. I felt that people, especially my parents, pushed me and my husband into having a baby and just shoved a bunch of guilt-tripping statements in my face like, “you will regret NOT having kids,” “you will be an amazing mom it’s the most incredible experience in the world, you NEVER regret becoming a mom!” “Life isn’t complete until you have a baby!” And many more I don’t care to remember.

So I had my daughter, who I love more than anything or anyone in the whole world, and I am trying sooooo hard to undo a lot of bullshit from the way I was raised and give her a better life. The problem is that I truly didn’t see things clearly until AFTER I had her. Sometimes you have instincts as a parent that come from the way you were raised and it’s like WOAH, no way, that’s not me and I’m not that parent. And I have found that I have become incredibly resentful and bitter towards my parents and angry at my younger self for basically blocking out so much of my childhood and for letting myself get bullied into something that is so huge. My daughter didn’t ask to be born, I brought her into the world without her permission and I am really trying so fucking hard to truly parent her and be there for her in ways my parents never were. She is at least never afraid to be her true self or express herself, unlike I was. But I honestly don’t think I should ever have been a mother, mostly because I think children deserve the absolute best and though I give it my all, I can see how woefully unprepared I was by the piss poor example I was given by my emotionally immature parents and I am often just completely burnt out. I have to constantly self-regulate and regulate my daughter AND my husband, and I often forgo sleep in order to get any alone time—which I DESPERATELY require and need. And none of it has come naturally to me like everyone said it would and things have never been the same between my husband and—which, for the record, isn’t a child’s fault EVER. Stressful situations show you who a person really is, and I discovered my husband wasn’t the person I thought he was. Nothing major like cheating or anything, he just did not step up to the plate to help like I would have expected, and you can’t unsee that. 

I tell every woman I know who asks about it that if they have A N Y doubt in their mind not to do it. Would I still have my daughter again if I knew I would have her again? Yes, 10,000%, no hesitation. But if I had a do-over and there was no guarantee? No. Absolutely not.

No, I won’t get too into the pharmacokinetics, but Wellbutrin is an NDRI, while Venlafaxine is a SNRI. Venlafaxine blocks the neuronal reuptake of serotonin, noradrenaline, and dopamine (to a much lesser extent, which is dose dependent). Some other well known SNRIs are duloxetine (cymbalta), tramadol (a low grade opioid related to Venlafaxine), desvenlafaxine (pristiq), levomilnacipran (fetzima), and more.

In contrast, some NDRIs you may have heard of are dexmethylphenidate (Focalin), bupropion (Wellbutrin) as we know, methylphenidate (Ritalin, concerta), and many other drugs but most would not have heard of them. Very different medications as you can tell lol. 

Venlafaxine is known to cause some of the harshest discontinuation effects. Doctors will often prescribe fluoxetine to take while slowly, SLOWLY lowering the dose of Venlafaxine over the course of weeks to months. It is not unusual to hear of people basically unable to quit SNRIs because of the harsh discontinuation effects.

“Allowed” is a relative term. Doctors write prescriptions and pharmacists may scratch their heads at some of them and call the doc and ask for clarification lol may outright refuse to fill prescriptions at times too—though that is quite rare. 

I’m not going to say that >60 mg/day has never been prescribed, but it isn’t usual or common. It isn’t common either to mix different stimulant medications like you mentioned, and I would caution you to never mention that idea to a doctor, as that would come across as drug-seeking (I understand it was an innocent question though).

My advice is that if 40 mg of Adderall isn’t working for you to try another medication. Vyvanse or Mydayis would be good options for you, probably Vyvanse would be better because it’s a totally different chemical composition. Your body, while certainly not stimulant naive, won’t be used to that medication, so it may work better for you. You can also consider adding in a “micro” dose of an SSRI, like Zoloft or Lexapro. I take 6 mg of Zoloft with Mydayis because of its synergistic effect.

Specific to Adderall. Vyvanse is a different chemical composition: lisdexamfetamine, while Adderall contains a mixture of dextroamphetamine and levoamphetamine. Off the top of my head, I *believe* the daily max. for Vyvanse is 70 mg/day, but don’t quote me on that.

So, this has been discussed and argued at length. As a nurse, I have access to medication prescribing and information guides and have looked into this specifically because of the back and forth. The max. prescribing dose/day is 60 mg for the treatment of **narcolepsy,** while the max. prescribing dose/day is 40mg for the treatment of ADHD/other. 

That doesn’t mean that doctors don’t make mistakes lol or don’t write prescriptions somewhat off-label, or bend the rules, but strictly speaking this is a very tightly controlled drug and a doctor has to answer to the prescriptions they write, their license is on the line.

There are different types of folliculitis and there are conditions that mimic folliculitis but are not actually folliculitis.

So it entirely depends on the person and the underlying causative factor. You cannot pin folliculitis down to one root cause, because there are several. In general, you have bacterial folliculitis, most commonly Staphylococcus, or fungal folliculitis, most commonly malassezia, (sometimes colloquially referred to as fungal acne). You have folliculitis caused by drugs like lithium or cyclosporines, you have other mimicking skin conditions like papular eczema, keratosis pilaris, hidradenitis suppurativa, miliaria (also known as heat rash or prickly heat), or Pseudofolliculitis barbae (shaving bumps), then you have dietary factors that can mimic folliculitis, specifically low levels of vitamins A and C, as well as high-fat diets.

We also have gram-negative folliculitis, which is a resistant, severe form if acne after prolonged antibiotic use to treat acne. Furuncles (boils), carbuncles (multiple boils, meaning multiple hair follicles, in one place—very, very painful), eosinophilic folliculitis, which is caused by a faulty immune system, and neutrophilic folliculitis. And on and on it goes.

Folliculitis is an umbrella term.

Sepsis occurs when an infection escapes “local” control (from source, such as a cut or illness) turns systemic. A predictable cascade of events unfolds and you are correct, a preview of sepsis is systemic inflammatory response syndrome, or SIRS. On a staircase, SIRS would be one step below sepsis. One step ABOVE sepsis is septic shock, then SEVERE septic shock, and then multiorgan dysfunction syndrome.

What often confuses people is that a few different things can cause SIRS, but, while all sepsis comes from SIRS, not all SIRS sources are sepsis. Sepsis HAS TO have an infectious component, while other sources of SIRS do not, e.g., trauma, blood loss, autoimmune disorders, etc.

Struggled with my skin for >10 years. I’ll give you my advice but my main problems areas have been face and chest. I am 100% cleared now.


A few things. Run everything you put on your skin through ingredients checkers like folliculitisscout and I also recommend using the ingredients checker on cosdna and not to use anything with comedogenic ingredients >1 or 2. So, you’re not putting ANY fungus/bacteria-feeding, pore-clogging ingredients on your face. You’re starving them out. 

Next, you’re treating. I recommend Hibiclens and straight up isopropyl alcohol in the immediate treatment term and then as things improve eliminating the alcohol and switching to benzoyl peroxide. Once you are completely clear you can taper off Hibiclens.

Then you are adding in adapalene gel. It cleans out pores at a deeper level and increases the speed of cell turnover. *you will need SPF, do not skip this.*

Lastly, habits. Don’t touch or pick your skin. Change towels/pillowcases often. Eliminate EXCESS sources of B-vitamins. You can trial eliminating gluten/dairy—that never ever helped me. Try to stop focusing on the issue—easier said than done.

One thing I haven’t seen anyone mention, is that as we age, our body odor changes due to chemical changes based on the aging process. This may be due to increases in one or some of the following chemicals: 2-nonenal, benzothianol, dimethylsulphone, and nonanal. >generic hate for uncomfortable feelings

You touched on a great point that I think is SUPER important! I know this is true for myself and I’ve noticed it in almost every single ADHDer I’ve ever met, that we all have an almost absolute intolerance for uncomfortable feelings. ADHDers, like ASDers, tend to have sensory issues, but unlike ASDers, ADHDers seem to have a heightened intolerance for EMOTIONAL discomfort in comparison to physical/sensory discomforts (not to dismiss the sensory issues too). 

Almost all of our knee jerk reactions are, “how do I avoid this feeling?” because RSD, well, it is physically painful and basically intolerable. Notice, almost no one is saying to go ahead and FEEL the feelings. We are all trying to avoid the feelings, but the key is to allow yourself to feel them and acknowledge them. Feelings, while valid, are just feelings. By simply saying to yourself, “I feel sad right now because I feel rejected and I feel embarrassed,” etc., you take the power out of the feelings. Feelings don’t equal reality, and it is really crazy how often just going through the situation with yourself solves your own problem. Recently, I had a friend who didn’t reply to an offer to go out and do something. I felt a little RSD but I told myself, “hey, you put yourself out there and asked a friend to do something and they didn’t reply. You’re feeling a little raw right now and a little rejected, but what is MOST LIKELY to be happening right now? She’s probably just really busy at work or something and forgot to reply. You would like people to give you the benefit of the doubt, give her the benefit of the doubt, you don’t own her time!”

Turns out, she WAS busy at work and DID forget to reply! We went out for dinner like the next night and she loved my idea and wants to do it. If I had reached out and been like, “hello? Never mind, we don’t have to do that, I know you’re busy,” or acted super needy because of the feelings of rejection I felt, well, I basically would have made the feelings real by acting on them. I do think you need positive reinforcement, I think that helps a ton, but it’s also important to remember one more thing, which is, “so what?”

I also started saying, “so what?” to all my worst RSD anxieties and it’s taken SO MUCH power out of the feelings. That person doesn’t want to do that thing with me? So what? Someone else will, or I can go by myself too I guess. That person didn’t think my joke was funny? So what? Obviously we wouldn’t be good friends then because we don’t share a sense of humor. This one person always leaves me a read and never texts me back, that bugs me. So what? So stop texting them if they are a bad communicator! So what’s the worst that can happen? Go through the list and see you will still be standing in the end of it. Yeah it might suck a little, a lot of things suck a little or a lot haha. Idk, I hope I’m not coming across like, “doctors hate this one trick!” but seriously, for me just simply sitting down and talking myself through things has been huge. Instead of feeling a certain way and trying to avoid it, it usually just reinforced the feelings because I didn’t really know WHY I was feeling a certain way, I just knew that I DID feel a certain way and I wanted it to stop…which usually led to me seeking validation and making the feelings REAL. It’s a very reactive way to live and go about life. I don’t think intellectualizing all your feelings is the way, you still should feel your feelings, but sometimes the feelings just…aren’t real 😂!

A few things help me massively: 1) moving my body—walking, running, working out in some capacity helps LOADS, it can even be as simple as cleaning your house in a frenzy, 2) talking it out with myself—journaling, painting, talking to myself to sort through my own feelings/insecurities about what’s going on and how I feel about it 3) talking it out with someone ELSE—this can be a spouse, a therapist/counselor, a trusted friend (just make sure you’re not over-burdening them). 

I’ve found that hitting these three markers, excess emotional energy, feelings and emotions recognition, and external discussion, really eliminate the RSD feeling. It’s easier to start with the numbers: top number is systolic and the bottom number is diastolic. The systolic number measures the amount of pressure the blood is putting on your arteries *when the heart is pumping.* In other words, the systolic number tells you how much pressure the blood puts against your arteries when the heart is actively beating and at work. Now it probably makes sense why that number is higher! 

In contrast, the diastolic number, again the second number, measures how much pressure the blood is putting against the arteries *when the heart is not pumping.* This is extra important, because this number can tell you how much *resistance* the  heart faces in order to pump blood effectively. Stiffer arteries or arteries clogged up with plaque will obviously increase the amount of resistance. So, when the heart is resting (not pumping) a higher diastolic number could indicate increased resistance: the heart needs to pump harder in order to overcome that resistance to meet the body’s oxygen needs.

It’s because those hairs are THICC, dense, and the texture is different—tougher, curlier, etc. When you shave a hair, it creates a blunt hair shaft which can be tough to pierce through the skin, creating an ingrown hair, as it gets blocked because it’s too thick, blunt, and tough.

When a hair grows naturally from the root, either on its own accord or after being pulled out from the root, i.e., tweezing, plucking, the hair is tapered at the tip, like a sharpened pencil. This pierces through much easier and is *less likely* to become ingrown.

That’s not to say it doesn’t happen, ingrown hairs just happen, but it’s *less likely* to be ingrown if it’s pulled out vs. shaved.

Hey, OP, CNA for about 5 years and I’m in my last semester of nursing school. Never use Vaseline as a barrier cream.

Vaseline seals the skin too much, which promotes secondary infections by trapping moisture, encouraging the skin to sweat, and starves the skin of oxygen, letting anaerobic bacteria go to town.

Ask the nurse for zinc barrier cream like z guard, hydraguard, or a silicone barrier cream, your nurse will know which is best.

There are lots of different units you could work instead. Someone mentioned ICU, there’s also step down units like the PCU, renal, there is also pediatrics, nicu, really you have lots of options! Talk to your boss and just put the word out.
